title: Should Young Children Spend More Time at School
paragraphs: In South Korea, there is a debate about whether the youngest elementary school students should spend more time at school.

At the moment, regular classes for first- and second-graders end at around 1 p.m. Many children then go to a state-run after-school care program, which usually finishes by 3 p.m. After that, many children go to private academies called "hagwons," or to art or sports programs.

South Korea's National Education Commission is now considering longer school days for first- and second-graders. At a meeting in September 2026, one researcher suggested slowly increasing the number of lessons for these students until it matches that of older children.

Supporters say Korean children spend less time in class than children in many other countries. According to researchers, first- and second-graders in South Korea receive 581 hours of lessons a year. This is 234 hours fewer than the average of 815 hours in OECD countries. In comparison, Japan and Germany require 768 and 774 hours.

Supporters also say that the short school day is hard for working parents. According to a government survey, 46% of families in which both parents work use hagwons mainly for childcare. Supporters believe that longer school days could reduce families' need for private academies.

However, teachers' unions are against the plan. One union called it a "trick" to make teachers do childcare work. Some teachers say that first-graders already find it hard to sit through five lessons a day. One union member also said that the plan would not solve the problem. Instead, children would simply start going to hagwons at 4 p.m. instead of 1 p.m.
Some teachers have suggested other ideas, such as smaller classes and special play spaces for young children.
No decision has been made yet. The question remains whether more time in class would really be better for young children.
